texts.orig: With the development of Metaverse technology, the avatar in Metaverse has faced serious security and privacy concerns. Analyzing facial features to distinguish between genuine and manipulated facial videos holds significant research importance for ensuring the authenticity of characters in the virtual world and for mitigating discrimination as well as preventing malicious use of facial data. To address this issue, the Facial Feature Points and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) deepfake video detection model is designed based on the clues of different FFPs distribution in real and fake videos and different displacement distances of real and fake FFPs between frames. The face video input is first detected by the BlazeFace model, and the face detection results are fed into the FaceMesh model to extract 468 FFPs. Then, the Lucas-Kanade (LK) optical flow method is used to track the points of the face, the face calibration algorithm is introduced to re-calibrate the FFPs, and the jitter displacement is calculated by tracking the FFPs between frames. Finally, the Ch is designed in the transformer, and the FFPs and FFP displacement are jointly classified through the ChT model. In this way, the designed ChT classifier is able to accurately and effectively identify deepfake videos. Experiments on open datasets clearly demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization capabilities of our approach.

texts.orig: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has resulted in the widespread integration of Metaverse technology into various aspects of entertainment, daily life, and education. Within this Metaverse environment, avatars confront substantial security and privacy challenges. Due to the close correlation between facial features and identity information, it is crucial to establish effective privacy protection measures through the analysis of facial features. By detecting forged faces in the virtual world, it is possible to identify manipulated faces with malicious and discriminatory intent, aiming to prevent gender, race, ethnic, and other imbalances. Simultaneously, Deepfake (DF) detection can be utilized to authenticate avatars, preventing identity theft or the deceptive misuse of avatars. If an avatar is identified as fake or manipulated, appropriate actions can be taken to mitigate potential risks.

texts.orig: Currently, DF videos, generated through adversarial networks, demonstrate an unprecedented level of authenticity. In the Metaverse, these DF creations typically fall into three primary categories: audio, video, and image manipulations, with video manipulations being the most widely recognized. This technique involves recording an individual and seamlessly replacing their facial features with those of another person using pre-existing video footage. This intricate process heavily relies on deep learning algorithms, which effectively blend facial images and videos to produce counterfeit content that is often imperceptible to the naked eye. It's worth noting that current DF technology primarily relies on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and its optimization models for its operation, representing a critical aspect of its functionality. ProGAN [10] and StyleGAN [16] are the two primary methods used to generate new synthetic faces. Fake videos are mainly divided into face replacement and expression exchange. Representative face replacement models include DeepFaceLab [34], FaceSwap (FS) [20], Face Swapping GAN [32], and DFs [19]. These models generate new synthetic videos by blending the image of a target person with existing video footage. DF, also known as facial reproduction, is currently popular with techniques, such as Face2Face (F2F) [44] and NeuralTextures (NTs) [43], where a facial expression from another person's face is replaced with the target's facial expression, such as changing the expression and movement to complete a fake "speech." The extensive application of DF technology, as evident from this, may pose significant security and privacy risks to virtual characters within the Metaverse.

texts.orig: Given the aforementioned background, DF videos can be utilized to steal the identities of virtual characters in the Metaverse. They can impersonate individuals for fraudulent activities, damage others' reputations, and initiate malicious cybersecurity attacks. This may ultimately lead to a crisis of trust in virtual world technology. Many experts and scholars have conducted research in this field. Currently, there are two main methods for detecting DF videos. The first method is based on analyzing single frames of the video to determine whether it is real or fake by examining details, such as hair, pupil, and facial features. The work presented in this article is inspired by Sun et al. [41], who demonstrated that the jitter of facial key points between real and fake video frames differs, as illustrated in Figure 1. Thus, a combination of Facial Feature Points (FFPs) distribution and displacement jitter is utilized to predict whether a video is real or fake.

texts.orig: We design a DF detection model FFPs and Class-head-Transformer (FFP-ChT) for the Metaverse, which focuses on identifying inconsistencies between the distribution of FFPs on a face and the jitter displacements in real and fake videos. Our model classifies videos based on the distribution of FFPs and the jitter displacements between those points in each video frame, thereby determining whether the face in the video is real or fake. FFP-ChT consists of three parts, first, a FFPs extraction model is used to extract 468 individual FFPs in each frame of the video. Secondly, the movement displacement of FFPs is calculated using the LK optical flow tracking method. Finally, the ChT is used to jointly predict FFPs and their jitter displacement in each video frame. Experimental results show that our DF detection model is robust and achieves higher Accuracy (ACC) not only on simple videos but also on higher resolution video datasets. texts.label: text
texts.orig: Similar to other AI tasks, the initial detection of fake face videos using single frame images has evolved from traditional methods to deep learning methods. Traditional methods include support vector machines [30], co-occurrence matrices [29], residual domain differences [21], and spectral differences [33] and have progressed to optical response heterogeneity and analysis of spatial domain features in images [37].
texts.text: Similar to other AI tasks, the initial detection of fake face videos using single frame images has evolved from traditional methods to deep learning methods. Traditional methods include support vector machines [30], co-occurrence matrices [29], residual domain differences [21], and spectral differences [33] and have progressed to optical response heterogeneity and analysis of spatial domain features in images [37].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In the deep learning-based models, Jeon et al. introduced the Transferable GAN-images Detection framework, which applied transfer learning to GAN for the first time in generating image detection [14]. Further, Jeon proposed the fine-tuning neural network architecture, Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network, that incorporated a self-attention module to focus on the module and the undersampling layer. This method significantly enhanced the ACC [15]. Chen et al. found that both the luminance and chrominance components play important roles in detecting GAN-generated facial images. Therefore, considering both the luminance and chrominance components in the dual-color spaces can enhance the robustness of the model [5]. Hsu et al. utilized pair learning to detect deep forged images and transformed DenseNet into a two-flow network structure, which inputted paired information to train the common pseudo-feature network. The paired information then connected to the classification layer to detect the authenticity of the input image. It was noted that images generated by different GAN may have unknown image distortion, such as blur, noise, and JPEG compression [13]. Liu et al. found that large texture information is more robust to image distortion and proposed the GramNet model, which focuses on texture information as an essential clue for deep forgery image detection [27]. When new DF generation methods become available, many DF detection models' performance deteriorates. Thus, Khalid et al. proposed One-Class FakeDetect, which uses variational autoencoder to encode inputs as distributions in potential spaces [18]. Hinton et al. proposed a robust architecture composed of multiple capsules to solve the limitations of neural networks on inverse image problems. Capsule networks were applied to deep forgery detection [36]. Dual Spatial Pyramid for Exposing Face Warp Artifacts (DSP-FWA) model of Li et al. was limited by computational resources and production time, as the DF algorithm could only synthesize face images of fixed size and had to be affine distorted to match the face configuration of the source. This distortion can leave noticeable artifacts due to the inconsistent resolution between the distorted facial area and the surrounding environment. And real face videos and fake face videos can be classified by artifact analysis [23].

texts.orig: Liu et al. proposed a new block shuffling framework that consists of intra-block and inter-block transfer learning modules. The former improves the robustness of the network by intra-block transformation and overfits the problem by adversarial learning, while the latter encourages the network to learn local features through interblock shuffling and to model the semantic relevance of local features through refactoring [26]. The model high-frequency proposed by Luo et al. in 2021 improved the detection ACC by designing a multi-scale high-frequency feature extraction module, residual-guided spatial attention module, and cross-modal attention module [28]. Liu et al. proposed the Spatial-Phase Shallow Learning (SPSL) model, which captures upsampled artifacts of face forgery, improving the portability of face forgery detection [25]. Chen et al. proposed a Multi-Scale Patch Similarity Module (MPSM) to measure the similarity between local regional features and form a robust generalized similarity model [7]. They also proposed enhancing the "diversity" of forgery by synthesizing enhanced forgery with a pool of forgery configurations and enhancing the "sensitivity" to forgery by forcing models to predict forgery configurations [6]. Li et al. proposed the face X-ray model, which can classify true and false face videos by capturing the mixed boundary of forged images and the non-mixed boundary of real images. DF detection has typically been described as a classification problem based on cross-entropy loss, which emphasizes class-level differences rather than essential differences between real and fake faces, limiting the model's generalization in the invisible domain [22]. Sun et al. proposed a new face forgery detection framework called Dual Contrast Learning (DCL), which addresses the problem of local content inconsistency by constructing local region pairs in the instance. The issue of local content inconsistency is addressed by constructing local region pairs within the instance [39]. Gu et al. proposed the Hierarchical Contrastive Inconsistency Learning model, which can distinguish real faces from fake faces by deeply contrasting images [12]. In the 2022 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), Shiohara proposed a novel composite training data called Self-Blended Images (SBIs) for detecting deep forgeries. The main idea behind SBIs is to enhance the robustness of the detection model by generating fake samples that are challenging to identify [38]. Chen et al. proposed a privacy-preserving model, Secure DeepFake Detection Network, which can detect DF faces without disclosing any private inputs, thus enhancing the privacy protection of facial data [4].

texts.orig: 2.2 Detection of DF Videos Based on Spatio-Temporal Features of Videos
texts.text: 2.2 Detection of DF Videos Based on Spatio-Temporal Features of Videos

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compared to DF detection based on image detail features, there have been fewer studies on DF detection based on video timing features, and the research in this area is relatively new. In light of the spatio-temporal inconsistency present in generated forged videos, Zhang et al. proposed a time-domain separation three-dimensional convolutional neural network, Temporal Dropout 3DCNN, which utilizes the inconsistent cues between video frames. This method exhibits excellent generalization ability and ACC compared to popular benchmarks [46]. Zheng et al. proposed an end-to-end framework comprising a full-time convolutional network. They focused on making the network learning time-agnostic and proposed to limit the ability of the network to handle spatial correlation. By limiting the spatial dimension, the network's evolution concentrates on time dependence. This method achieves better results in dataset training without any pre-training or manual operation [48]. In 2022, Zhang et al. proposed a simple yet effective patch-level method, spatio-temporal dropout Transformer, to fully utilize the spatio-temporal inconsistencies present in local facial areas of different frames in DF videos. The input video is extracted into a facial frame sequence, which is then reassembled into a patch pack and introduced into the visual converter to learn the differential representation of dynamic spatio-temporal cues in local facial areas describing different frames [47]. In 2021, Sun et al. proposed a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) classification algorithm model, LRNet, based on 68 human face landmarks, and introduced a new plug-and-play landmark calibration module to improve the ACC of facial geometric features and the effectiveness of time modeling [41]. Gu et al. studied the local motion of the image extensively and proposed a new sampling unit, Intra-Snippet Inconsistency Module, which uses bidirectional time difference operation and a learnable convolution kernel to mine short-term motion within each fragment. Their Snippet Inconsistency Module model achieved robust results in detecting DF videos [11]. In 2023, Sun proposed the FTDN model, which is based on facial areas such as displacement path to detect manipulated videos. This method can robustly identify displacement information [40].
texts.text: Compared to DF detection based on image detail features, there have been fewer studies on DF detection based on video timing features, and the research in this area is relatively new. In light of the spatio-temporal inconsistency present in generated forged videos, Zhang et al. proposed a time-domain separation three-dimensional convolutional neural network, Temporal Dropout 3DCNN, which utilizes the inconsistent cues between video frames. This method exhibits excellent generalization ability and ACC compared to popular benchmarks [46]. Zheng et al. proposed an end-to-end framework comprising a full-time convolutional network. They focused on making the network learning time-agnostic and proposed to limit the ability of the network to handle spatial correlation. By limiting the spatial dimension, the network's evolution concentrates on time dependence. This method achieves better results in dataset training without any pre-training or manual operation [48]. In 2022, Zhang et al. proposed a simple yet effective patch-level method, spatio-temporal dropout Transformer, to fully utilize the spatio-temporal inconsistencies present in local facial areas of different frames in DF videos. The input video is extracted into a facial frame sequence, which is then reassembled into a patch pack and introduced into the visual converter to learn the differential representation of dynamic spatio-temporal cues in local facial areas describing different frames [47]. In 2021, Sun et al. proposed a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) classification algorithm model, LRNet, based on 68 human face landmarks, and introduced a new plug-and-play landmark calibration module to improve the ACC of facial geometric features and the effectiveness of time modeling [41]. texts.orig: Our proposed DF video detection model FFP-ChT consists of four components as shown in Figure 2. Firstly, the input video is divided into frames, and a set of frames of the video image is fed into the BlazeFace model for face detection. The prediction results of FFPs and the prediction results of FFPs displacement sequences are combined to predict whether the input video is real or fake.

texts.orig: Celeb-DF [24] is a recently proposed dataset with high-visual quality. The Celeb-DF dataset comprises of two versions: Celeb-DF(v1) and Celeb-DF(v2). In this experiment, Celeb-DF(v2) version was used. Celeb-DF(v1) contains 158 real videos and 795 fake videos, while Celeb-DF(v2) is a significant expansion over the v1 version, with 5,639 fake videos and 590 real videos based on publicly available YouTube clips from 59 celebrities of various genders, ages, and races. The average length of all videos is about 13 seconds, with a standard frame rate of 30 frames per second; 56.8% of the videos feature male subjects and 43.2% feature female subjects. The age distribution is as follows: 8.5% of the subjects are aged 60 or older, 30.5% are aged 50-60, 26.6% are in their 40s, 28.0% are in their 30s, and 6.4% are under 30. The racial distribution is as follows: 5.1% of the subjects are Asian, 6.8% are African American, and 88.1% are Caucasian. Additionally, the dataset features a wide range of variations in face size (in pixels), orientation, lighting conditions, and backgrounds. The fake face videos were generated by swapping each pair of faces of 59 subjects using an improved DF algorithm. As a result, the overall visual quality of the Celeb-DF dataset is significantly improved compared to the existing datasets.

texts.orig: 4.2.1 Experimental Environment. The experiments presented in this article are conducted on the Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS operating system, utilizing a GeForce RTX 2080 Ti graphics processing unit with a graphics memory capacity of 12 GB. The CUDA version 9.2 and PyTorch 1.7.1 framework are utilized. The FF,, dataset is divided into a training set and a validation set using an 8:2 ratio, similar to the basic model. For the CelebDF dataset, the division method provided by the original authors is adopted. Additionally, the parameters used for all datasets are the same. The specific experimental parameters are set as follows: batch size of 1.024, learning rate of 0.001, 400 epochs for training the detection network based on the absolute location of key points, and 300 epochs for training the detection network based on the relative location of FFPs. During training, each video is divided into fixed 60 frame segments as a training sample. The key point information of each frame is mapped to a 128 dimensional vector, and position coding is carried out for each 60 frame training sample with a droprate of 0.1 for the position coding layer. Then, a Learnable embedding vectors (cls_token) is added, and the data are passed through a Transformer encoder with a dropout layer of droprate = 0.1 for encoding. The specific parameters for the Transformer encoder are set as follows: the encoder had 1 layer, 8 attention heads, 512 dimensions for each attention head, 128 for the last layer normalization, and 2 for the output of the linear transformation layer.

texts.orig: In this article, to improve face privacy protection in the virtual world, we presented a new method for detecting DF videos that focuses on the inconsistency between the distribution of FFPs and their jitter displacements in real and fake videos. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DF detection model has good robustness, as it achieves higher ACC in video datasets with higher resolution and obtains better detection results in simple videos. With the evolution of the Metaverse, in the future, DF detection can assist in establishing a series of identity verification standards in the virtual world to ensure the authenticity of users' identities. Simultaneously, it is possible to explore DF detection that combines various sensors and data sources to enhance the validation of real identities, thereby improving the capability to detect forged faces and reducing deception in virtual spaces.
